Business.title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
Business.text:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.

Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".

The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.

The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.

Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.

"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.

Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.

However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.

Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.

However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".

Inflation, which measures the pace of price rises over time, is well below its peak of a few years ago but remains above the Bank of England's 2% target and is expected to increase further next year.

Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September 2026, largely due to higher fuel prices. Millions of households are also set to be hit by energy bill increases in January.

Higher fuel prices can lead to prices rising for a host of goods and staples as businesses pass on higher costs to customers.

But the Bank said there was "limited evidence" this had happened so far for goods, such as food, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower margins.

In an interview with the BBC, Bailey defended the decision to raise rates despite the Bank's assessment that inflation was yet to spread to other parts of the economy.

He said further increases in energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and "that's what we have to seek to lean against".

Business.title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
Business.text:
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.

Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.

My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.

It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.

Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.

At least there is no blindfold.

The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.

Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.

And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.

The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.

Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.

Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency, with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.

So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.

The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

Business.title: UK interest rate rise: Three ways it could affect you
Business.text:
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.

Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.

Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.

Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.

This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.

Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.

Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.

Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.

That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.

"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.

"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."

The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.

So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.

When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.

The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.

Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.

"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.

The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.

The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.

About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.

Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.

An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.

If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.

While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.

The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.

Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

Business.title: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears
Business.text:
Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.

In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.

Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.

The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year.

The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.

In South Korea, the Kospi index plunged more than 8% at one point, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.

The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%.

European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback".

"The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added.

"The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off."

Business.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
Business.text:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.

Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.

Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".

In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.

These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, which can then be used to try and access their accounts.

Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.

It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts which contained personal images.

The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, which deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.

The incident led the firm to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.

Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.

"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.

The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.

It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, and said 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.

Business.title: Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy
Business.text:
It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.

Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.

Democrats would do well to recall that the affordability strains that helped deliver them to power are not dissimilar to those that delivered the presidency to Trump two years ago. And they could again quickly become their enemy.

“First, Americans want Washington to bring down the cost of living,” said Chuck Schumer, Senate majority leader-in-waiting. Likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries added that “we’ve promised to fight for an affordable America, and that’s exactly what we will do”. They will soon discover the limits to their power to undo Trump’s economic blunders and steer an economy that is largely driven by forces outside their control.

Take gas prices, the single most powerful motivation for voters’ rebellion against the Republicans enabling Trump’s policy choices. Reining them in will require reaching an understanding with Iran that reopens the strait of Hormuz. Schumer thinks Democrats can achieve that. “We are going to end the war,” he said.

Trump may disagree, however. And while it is true that Congress is legally entitled to end wars – it is the only branch of government entitled to start one – it is unclear what such legal niceties might mean in practice. Republicans have controlled Congress since Trump went to war. Still, he has pursued it without asking for their approval. Democrats could now try to cut war funding, but they do not have the requisite 60 Senate votes to prevent a filibuster.

Trump’s trade war has similar characteristics. When the supreme court struck down Trump’s “national security” tariffs because they exceeded presidential authority, the administration reimposed many of them under a different statute, deploying a new, also spurious rationale. There is also little that Democrats can do to stop Trump’s war on immigration. It is fully funded and can carry on unimpeded, further disrupting construction and other immigrant-reliant industries.

Even the low-hanging fruit hangs rather high. While it may seem easy to reinstate federal subsidies for health insurance programs under the Affordable Care Act, or undo or postpone cuts to Medicaid and food stamps in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats will be hard-pressed to find the money, given a budget deficit that is already running at a whopping 6% of the nation’s gross domestic product.

Just preventing further damage will be an uphill battle. A lame duck Trump who no longer feels the need to please voters is likely to give free rein to his most destructive urges. While Democrats will be able to block Trump’s new legislative proposals, they don’t have the votes to overcome presidential vetoes.

Optimists may believe that after Tuesday’s shellacking, sufficient Republicans in Congress could be convinced to buck their president’s wishes. But most of those who survived the bloodbath come from the most faithful Maga districts and states and are the least likely to abandon their leader.

The economy itself – driven almost exclusively by a frenzied artificial intelligence investment boom – is unlikely to help Democrats achieve their goal of easing voters’ economic strains.

Wall Street is already doubting that the massive investments to build data-processing centers to train powerful AI models will pay off in time to justify the money. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index has fallen by more than 10% in the last month.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the large AI hyperscalers have raised almost $200bn in bond markets so far this year, almost twice as much as in all of 2025. Altogether, the bank added, AI-related firms have raised nearly $500bn in debt so far in 2026.

Were this bubble to pop and the funding to stop, it would likely deliver an economic downfall to beat even the Great Recession sparked by the housing bubble in 2008. When the time comes, a government hamstrung by $40tn in debt and interest rates hovering near 20-year highs will have little fiscal space to soften the blow.

Can voters’ newfound love for Democrats survive the likely turbulence ahead? Justin Wolfers, an economist at the University of Michigan who runs Platypus Economics, observes that neither the unemployment rate nor inflation are bad enough to justify Americans’ extreme pessimism about the economy. So what’s driving the sour mood? A collapse in confidence in economic leadership.

Tuesday’s Republican bloodbath might, on its own, improve Americans’ spirits. Limited though their powers may be, Democrats will at least offer some resistance to Trump’s most destructive impulses. But the economy will likely pose a greater challenge for the new Democratic Congress than it has to the Republicans currently in charge. In two years’ time, Democrats might be facing anger over an economic scenario that has gotten palpably worse.

They might then come to embrace the limits of their power and hope voters blame the president – not Congress – for their economic unhappiness.

Business.title: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
Business.text:
The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.

Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.

Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.

Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.

The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.

“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”

But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.

In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.

Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Man City: Enzo Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare
Sports.text:
Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start as Manchester City manager is rapidly turning into a nightmare.

Amid a sea of noise from the home faithful on the banks of the River Trent, the delirious Forest supporters witnessed their side produce a thrilling performance as City sunk to a third straight Premier League loss.

Maresca's leaky backline continues to make defensive blunders and once Josko Gvardiol gave the ball away for Jair Cunha to open the scoring in the sixth minute, City were on the back foot.

With Arsenal edging past Hull earlier in the day and keeping another clean sheet, City head into the international break searching for answers after a 3-1 loss and six points behind the champions.

Maresca said: "The first half we didn't match [Forest's] intensity or win duels or second balls. The first thing required in these games is intensity.

"We tried to react at 2-0 but it's too late. We scored one, probably could have scored more but in transition we concede one more. No panic. We need to understand but no panic."

Asked why the intensity was low, Maresca replied: "I need to analyse that."

The situation already looks bleak for City, but what does history show?

Should Brighton fail to beat Brentford on Sunday, Arsenal would be just the fourth side in Premier League history to have a six-point lead after 10 games, while only two teams have been so far behind as City at this stage and gone on to win the title.

One of those was Manchester United in 2002-03. The other? City themselves in 2013-14 under Manuel Pellegrini.

But Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton have the opportunity to leap up to second place and five points behind the Gunners should they beat Brentford.

There is another factor which looms large over City's campaign.

The club have lodged an appeal after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules.

That process is ongoing - and it is not yet known what potential sanctions City could face.

But - even if any possible punishment does not affect this season - their title hopes are looking slimmer by the match.

With his hands tucked inside his trouser pockets and his head bowed, a forlorn-looking Maresca paced the touchline towards the end of the match.

The City boss said during the week he was still getting to know his players, but performances like the one against Forest will provide some clarity as to who he can, and cannot, trust.

After starting the season with seven straight wins, City have hit real trouble with defeats against Aston Villa, Brighton and now a pumped-up Forest.

Their problems at the back are not helping as it was another game where individual errors cost them dearly - and former striker Liam Delap took full advantage of the lapses in concentration with two goals.

Gvardiol was at fault for the first, Iliman Ndiaye and Elliot Anderson got in a muddle for the second, while Matheus Nunes did not put a challenge in for the third.

"Before the game all the talk was about individual errors," former Forest winger Steve Stone told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Apart from the first goal, this hasn't been about that - the line is disjointed.

"The full-backs were very wide. If the ball turns over quickly and you pass it with your first pass you can be right through them. They have been exposed today.

"Oliver Glasner's team have played through them every time."

It was a miserable return to the City Ground for Anderson since his £116m move to City in the summer and the midfield dynamic alongside Enzo Fernandez does not seem to be working.

The Argentine should have scored with a headed chance from close range but spent much of the game complaining in referee Sam Barrott's ear - City team-mates and supporters may be expecting more from their club record signing.

The former Chelsea player scored in the midweek Champions League win at RB Leipzig, but that is his only goal or assist in his past nine games.

Maresca needs to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez during the international break.

Stone added: "I came here tonight thinking City would win, I thought they had chances. This is a real hammer blow to them, there is something not right about the back four at the minute.

"I have never seen a City team give the ball away so much in the middle of the park."

Rayan Cherki's stunning strike gave City hope but they could not turn it around and the numbers following the result make for grim:

City have lost three consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run of four in November-December 2024

They have become the second team in English top-flight history - after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 - to win their first seven games of a season and then lose their next three

This was their first league defeat by two or more goals against a side starting the day in the relegation zone since November 2008 (a 2-0 loss to Bolton Wanderers).

Maresca was forced to chop and change his defence again, withdrawing both Gvardiol and Marc Guehi at half-time because of injuries, according to the manager.

It meant Nunes came in at right-back, with Abdukodir Khusanov moving inside, and Nico O'Reilly playing down the left.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport: "I thought City's performance was poor in terms of mentality.

"To make so make so many mistakes when you go anywhere in the Premier League, but especially to a team who are fighting for the lives, and you know they're going to come after you.

"They were sloppy with the ball, not winning duels. I would even probably go as far as saying there was probably a bit of arrogance at the start of the game from them.

"I think that there are now some big questions to ask the manager about how he gets them back on track. I think with the talent they have got, it is not going to be a big problem.

"But I think defensively, maybe sticking to the same backline for a little while is the way forward."

Sports.title: Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Martin Odegaard spare VAR blushes?
Sports.text:
It was not pretty, but Martin Odegaard's goal was enough to secure the 1-0 win that ensured Arsenal go into the international break as the Premier League leaders.

It was Arsenal's 34th 1-0 win under Mikel Arteta, to equal their best start to a Premier League season under the Spaniard of 27 points earned after 10 games in 2022-23.

No team has enjoyed more 1-0 wins since Arteta was appointed back in 2019, with the Gunners winning their past 10 home games in all competitions, keeping eight clean sheets in that time.

Odegaard's goal though, bundled home from close range, may well have been a relief to those at Pro Ref, too.

A controversial video assistant referee (VAR) decision, which denied the Gunners a first-half penalty, threatened to be the story as a largely uneventful game drifted by.

When referee Farai Hallam was sent to the pitchside monitor for a VAR review for a shirt pull by Nobel Mendy on Kai Havertz, surely everyone inside the Emirates was expecting a penalty.

The irony would not be lost on Liverpool fans, who were denied a VAR penalty for a shirt pull last weekend when Arsenal's Jurrien Timber tugged back Alexander Isak.

Unlike Isak, Havertz made sure everyone - including VAR Michael Oliver, was aware that a defender had hold of his shirt.

Indeed, the cheers had already begun when Hallam started to describe the foul to the crowd - but Gunners supporters were stopped in their tracks. The referee pivoted to an offside against Havertz, and play restarted with a free-kick to Hull.

Had Arsenal not mustered that 72nd-minute winner from their captain, much of the attention would, once again, have been on VAR.

If Arsenal had dropped points, it wouldn't have been the first time this weekend that a match would have been dominated by discussions about the video officials.

On Friday, Coventry City were denied what appeared to be a clear penalty against Everton for a hair pull by James Tarkowski on Caleb Yirenkyi. Then in the second half, when Thierno Barry scored to put the Toffees 2-1 up and the ball appeared to come off his hand.

The controversy continued in Saturday's early kick-off between Leeds and Tottenham. First, Leeds wanted a penalty for handball by Mateus Fernandes, though replays did show the ball hit the Spurs player's shoulder.

Then came the potential red card for a challenge by Jayden Bogle on Mathys Tel, which has split opinion. The VAR, Tony Harrington, eventually decided after a four-minute VAR check that the foul did not have enough force.

That Tel was forced off injured, and referee John Brooks did not even show a yellow card on the field, only added to the frustration for Tottenham.

So on to the Emirates, and again the debate was around VAR.

It's a situation few would question. After all, an offside player winning a penalty surely goes against the very logic of the law?

If an offside player is running to the ball and is fouled before they attempt to play the ball or challenge an opponent, then the foul is considered to come before the offside offence.

The law seeks to prevent situations whereby defenders have carte blanche to foul attackers, just because the opponent is offside.

Former Darren Cann told BBC Match of the Day: “The foul should have taken precedence over the offside and it should have been a penalty. The law is very ambiguous though.”

But is a complex area of law and is very much open to interpretation.

We have a few past case studies.

In February 2019, the season before VAR came in, an offside Harry Kane was awarded a late penalty in a north London derby after being dragged down by Shkodran Mustafi.

Two years ago, Newcastle were awarded a spot-kick against Bournemouth through a VAR intervention when Adam Smith tugged back an offside Fabian Schar.

Yet last December, after being awarded a penalty against Leeds, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was ruled to be offside and the spot-kick ruled out through VAR.

So which interpretation is correct? Kane and Schar, or Havertz and Ouattara?

Ouattara was somewhat different, as he appeared to be engaging with Gabriel Gudmundsson as the ball was played.

The Havertz example is more like the one involving Schar, who was running forward when his shirt was tugged back.

But there is an additional consideration, and this is where Oliver's thinking will lie.

Officials are asked to consider the likelihood of the attacker becoming involved in the play from a second phase. Let's say the ball could be first played by a team-mate, which then makes them onside. Then they are not purely benefitting from being offside.

In the case of Schar and Kane, they could have benefitted from that second phase.

Havertz was the only attacker who had any chance of being involved in the play, so the VAR determined offside was the fair outcome.

Confused? You've got every right to be.

At least tonight most of the talk will be about another victory for Arsenal - and not VAR.

Another game, another win but still Arsenal are looking for their attack to spark into life.

At the end of the day results matter but Arsenal, despite being top, are the lowest scorers of the teams in the top four.

They have the best defence in the league and arguably Europe but goals are also seeming hard to come by at the other end.

Arsenal have not scored more than twice in the league since the opening day of the season, when they put three past Coventry.

Arteta's side are missing talisman Bukayo Saka, who is out with a quadricep injury, and has a unique partnership with Ben White and Martin Odegaard on the right.

On the left Christos Tzolis started the season well but, after a hamstring injury while playing for Greece, the 24-year-old has not looked the same threat.

The same can be said for Kai Havertz too.

The 27-year-old picked up a hamstring injury playing for Germany and, even though he scored the winner against Liverpool, his performances have not reached the same level.

Viktor Gyokeres is firmly second choice this season and Arteta is still working out how to get the best out of the maverick Eberechi Eze, while Noni Madueke is working to fill the gap left by Saka.

Arteta was asked about the number of single-goal wins this season and what he can do to improve that.

"To be more efficient," was the answer the Gunners boss gave. "We are one against one against the keeper. That's happened twice today.

"There is a penalty there, there is another situation inside the box where the ball is bouncing. So many shots that have been deflected, blocked. We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic.

"Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that, and that's it. And open, I think, score much earlier because obviously that's going to change the course of the game."

Even if the Gunners could be more free-flowing going forward, they have started the season in a formidable way - winning nine of their 10 league games.

And if they manage to keep up that rate of winning, the Gunners will likely defend their Premier League crown and win back-to-back titles for the first time in 100 years.

Sports.title: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Lando Norris and George Russell hoping for more rain in race after wet qualifying
Sports.text:
Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday.

It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it.

Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme.

Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning.

"When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it.

"It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with.

"I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high."

The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row.

Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year.

Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage.

Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect.

Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions.

"We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace.

"We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it.

"I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly.

"These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well.

"It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake.

"But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding."

For Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them.

Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history.

Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector.

The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened.

He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second.

It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest.

But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second.

"Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying."

He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there.

"In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."

The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created.

With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light.

This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it.

Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again.

"We took some risks in Q1, in Q2, where the conditions were a little bit unknown for everybody and we made it through and then our first Q3 of the year, so obviously pleased with that," Alonso said.

"Then in Q3 I was expecting maybe a little bit more. I was first on the queue. But the tyres were ice cold in Q3, so I had no grip.

"But yeah, I look at the times now, I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me. So yeah, it's way too much, you know, in front to really dream about any higher positions.

"There is less time full throttle (in the wet), because there is no grip. So obviously they cannot exploit the extra power.

"But still the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners. We still have a little bit of an issue there.

"But no, I think these conditions is more about the level of risk you want to take. There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there."

Alonso joins Norris and Russell in hoping for a wet race, feeling that if it's dry he will inevitably sink back to Aston Martin's natural level, especially with the long pit straight where Honda's lack of power will render him defenceless.

The race promises much with Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all aiming to make progress from the back, even if the drivers feel that overtaking at Interlagos will be harder in this year's new-style cars than before.

For Ferrari, it has been a difficult weekend, that started with clear-the-air talks between Leclerc and Hamilton after their first-lap battle cost them victory in Mexico last weekend.

Both took new internal combustion engines, which gave them 10-place grid penalties, and then Hamilton's brand new one broke in final practice. So Ferrari gave him another one, leaving him at the back with Verstappen.

The two multiple champions will be in competition to see who can make progress faster, and perhaps Ferrari are not so unhappy that Hamilton and Leclerc are separated by six places on the grid.

Both drivers said all was well after their chat on Thursday evening.

Leclerc - who returned to Europe between the two races to be at the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca - said: "It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long.

"At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and it will be important to look ahead.

"I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away. Of course, there is tension. Of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those then helps a whole lot."

Hamilton added: "Me and Charles sat and spoke and we squashed it, and we're moving on.

"We still have a huge amount of respect for each other and I'm glad we had a chat and now we move on.

"We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes in those scenarios it takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side.

"It's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other."

Sports.title: Buatsi vs Hutchinson 2: Scotland's Willy Hutchinson wins WBC light-heavyweight title
Sports.text:
Willy Hutchinson was crowned the WBC light-heavyweight champion after he produced the performance of his career to beat Joshua Buatsi in Manchester.

Hutchinson, 28, edged the tense rematch with the judges scoring it 117-112, 115-113, 115-113 to avenge his defeat by Buatsi in 2024.

Saturday's contest was initially for the interim title but was upgraded when American David Benavidez gave up the WBC gold to move up to cruiserweight.

It was a childhood dream come true for Scotland's Hutchinson, who said before the fight he wrote about his dreams of becoming a WBC champion at the age of 13.

An emotional Hutchinson said after his win was confirmed: "I want to tell the story one more time. I was 13-years-old. My dad was working in Sweden. I signed it in a book, I said I will become a world champion. Let's go!

"Can I say thank you to my coach because I'll you one thing, without him I don't think I'll be here today let alone boxing. This man dug me out of a hole that I never thought that I would get out of, so this is all a bonus baby."

Ticket sales were modest for a world title fight as it was clear that it did not capture the attention of the British public. But those inside made the atmosphere as raucous as possible, with the Manchester crowd favouring Hutchinson.

And they were delighted when the result was read out and Hutchinson became the eighth British light-heavyweight champion - the first since Nathan Cleverly in 2017.

Hutchinson improved his record to 21 victories with two defeats, while it is the second time Londoner Buatsi has lost in 22 professional fights.

Fight week was dominated by predictions that Buatsi, five years Hutchinson's senior, is over the hill.

And the Londoner did nothing to prove otherwise as Hutchinson often toyed with his opponent in the centre of the ring.

The first fight in 2024 had Buatsi walking to the ring as a comfortable favourite, and he backed that up with crushing body shots to send Hutchinson tumbling twice.

But this time around, Hutchinson was a different fighter. In his own words, he had "matured" after picking up two wins since last facing Buatsi.

Hutchinson clearly had the crowd on his side as he made the walk to cheers, while Buatsi was met by a chorus of boos as he paraded around the ring before the bell.

For Buatsi, the strategy was very much the same as the first encounter - whip shots into the body - but Hutchinson now had answers.

The AO Arena is famous for its boxing nights with the city's favourite boxing son, Ricky Hatton, becoming world champion here for the first time in June 2005 in a thriller against Kostya Tszyu.

This did not reach those heights, as the upper tier was closed off because of a lack of ticket sales - and fans of Manchester's Jack Rafferty departed after he won the co-main event.

This did not deter Hutchinson from advancing in the latter rounds and landing rapid triple jabs, while also switching stances.

As Manchester royalty Bez, of the Happy Mondays, watched on from ringside, Hutchinson's corner told him "three rounds and you're a world champion" after the ninth.

And they were right. Despite Buatsi's advances late on, Hutchinson held out to become world champion for the first time.

Sports.title: Dewi Lake says Wales let themselves down in Japan win
Sports.text:
Captain Dewi Lake says Wales let themselves down during the lacklustre 28-21 Nations Championship victory against Japan in Cardiff.

Josh Adams added two tries to scores from prop Archie Griffin and wing Louis Rees-Zammit as Wales claimed a bonus-point win.

This was their second victory from four games in the competition but Lake was left frustrated with aspects of the performance.

"There were massive parts of that game where we let ourselves down," he said.

"Getting into camp, we said we were going to do things that we probably didn't do against Japan.

"That's disappointing but this is a group that wants to grow and will challenge each other."

In front of a crowd of 52,425 supporters, Wales had to hold on for only the fourth win in Steve Tandy's 13 Tests in charge, two of which have come against Japan.

Lake said a victory should not be underestimated with Wales having suffered recent losing streaks, which included a record 18 consecutive Test defeats in a row.

"A win is massive for this group, for the confidence and trust we'll get in each other," he said.

"We were happy with the win and it's something we've not done often enough, so I am proud of the boys."

Wales remain fifth in the northern hemisphere table but face much tougher challenges this month.

New Zealand, fresh from defeating Scotland, are the visitors to Cardiff next Saturday before Australia play at the Principality Stadium on 21 November.

"If you look at the two Test matches, we did things today that weren't good enough to compete in those games," said Lake.

"We'll have to get a lot right next week and fix some stuff."

Head coach Tandy said he was expecting more from his side this weekend.

"It's good to start the campaign with a bonus-point win but I can't run away from the performance when I talk about it," said Tandy.

"There are elements of the performance we definitely need to improve. I thought we'd be better than that in some elements.

"There was good stuff from us, in terms of the line breaks and how we opened Japan up, but we weren't ruthless enough.

"We'll definitely have to do that for the next couple of games but it helps to review after a win."

Japan head coach Eddie Jones said it was an opportunity missed to win a first game in Cardiff against Wales.

"That could have been a historic win for us but you've got to be good enough to take advantage of those mistakes," he said.

"We weren't quite good enough and it was certainly a missed opportunity."

Jones said he was proud of his young team but believes they needed to be more clinical.

"If you watch rugby now, once you get in the 22 and if you don't take points from that, that's the difference in the game," said Jones.

"We had three opportunities but we didn't take chances and Wales did. Their points-per-entry was higher than ours."

Jones questioned some aspects of the interpretation of New Zealand referee Paul Williams at the contact area.

"I hope I'm not going to get in trouble for this but there was one penalty for not supporting your weight at the breakdown and it was against us," said Jones.

"Anyone watching that game, can you think there was just one ruck where the supporting player was off his feet?

"That can be the difference between winning and losing.

"I'm not complaining, I'm just saying sometimes you don't get the rub of the green.

"That can happen. You've got to suck it up and get on with it. Actually maybe I am complaining!"

Japan travel to face Jones' former England side at Allianz Stadium at Twickenham next Saturday.

Sports.title: Scotland's familiar frailties brutally exposed in All Blacks schooling
Sports.text:
Fair play to the All Blacks. At least this time they didn't wait until the closing minutes to put Scotland away, they took them out of their misery way earlier than that. A small mercy, in a sense.

No dramas, no late moments of All Black genius required, no clutch try to swing it in the end and break Scottish hearts. Those late sucker-punches? They're the worst.

It's easier this way. You know where you are with shellackings. It's the near misses that are harder to take.

If you're going to lose to the All Blacks, maybe it's better to be routed than robbed, better to be outclassed than walking away with a sense of grievance or a feeling a win was left behind.

This was a systematic dismantling, all over in the 51st minute when Beauden Barrett, as much of a genius now at the age of 35 as he ever was, scored his second try of the day.

Barrett is now on 50 Test tries and 148 caps. Murrayfield witnessed one of the all-time greats on Saturday; classy, intelligent and ruthless. Any notion Scotland could bring an end to 121 years without a win against New Zealand was trampled underfoot by Barrett and his band of brothers; blood brothers and otherwise.

The first half was a thrill-fest, the second half was an annihilation. At the break, with Ewan Ashman having completed his hat-trick and Murrayfield rocking, the great Richie McCaw stood away to the side, just below the media gantry.

Was he ashen-faced - or Ashman-faced - at the space Scotland were finding and the tries they were scoring? Was he fretful this just might be the day the record tumbles?

Er, no. He took out his phone and started tapping in the manner of a guy ordering a taxi - for Scotland, of course. McCaw, and every All Black in his wake, don't worry in moments like this.

They just up the ante and back themselves. They increase the intensity, the accuracy, the power. They feast on mistakes and accelerate away.

The second half was 19-0 to the All Blacks. That's what outstanding rugby teams do. Away from home against a dangerous team in front of a loud crowd. They embrace adversity. They get turned on by it.

Dave Rennie's favourite word, in a rugby context, is brutal, as in brutal physicality, brutal execution, brutal in putting a foot on an opponent's throat and keeping it there. All of that was visited upon Scotland. New Zealand were better and smarter. Their rugby IQ was on a different level.

Gregor Townsend and his players spoke later about where it all went wrong. Didn't take enough of their chances in the first half, didn't make it hard enough for New Zealand to get field position, didn't survive at the breakdown, didn't deliver on discipline, didn't look after ball.

All true, but the greater truth is that after three close Tests under Townsend since 2017, New Zealand have now pulled miles clear of Scotland.

Townsend can talk about all the little things and some of the big things Scotland got wrong but these things didn't suddenly afflict his team. They didn't just drop out of the sky. They're in the DNA of this team. We have seen these failings before in defeat and even in victory.

Scotland's attack can be a thing of wonder, capable of creating space and delivering sensational tries against the very best teams on the planet. They did it on Saturday against the All Blacks, they did it against South Africa in July, they did it against France and Ireland in March. These are good rugby players.

The elite teams pride themselves on defence - and that's where Scotland are mired in quicksand. They conceded five tries in defeat to the Pumas last autumn. In victory, they put 50 on France but conceded 40 points and six tries.

They shipped 43 points against Ireland and another six tries. They lost 42-18 to the Boks in the summer and gave up another six tries. They beat the Pumas but, again, their inability to be savage on the other side of the ball saw them conceding 38 points and five tries. It was another 40-pointer against the All Blacks - and another six tries.

There were lovely moments in all of those Tests, but Scotland's big mantra coming into the autumn was all about making life difficult for opponents, making sure every yard they made in possession was only won after a battle, every try they scored was only achieved after fighting for their lives through the phases.

Worthy sentiments and an important mission statement, but four minutes into it on Saturday, New Zealand threw a bit of trickery at Scotland at a lineout and scored with ease.

The piece of deception - two runners bolting off a lineout as decoy men - has been done by a few teams already this season. It wasn't a revelation but it was enough to fool Scotland.

The irony came in the name of the scorer. Scotland wanted their defence to be Braveheart in its, well, brutality. Wallace Sititi scored that first try. The back-row was named after William Wallace. So much for freedom from concession of soft scores.

The All Blacks got to 43 points with 12 minutes left. They could have had more, but they'd made their point. They're back. Not at Springbok level, clearly, but improving.

Rennie, and his sidekick Mike Blair, have brought huge improvement in a relatively short time. These All Blacks are light years ahead of the version Scott Robertson brought here 12 months ago.

Townsend must now piece together shattered morale and go again next Sunday. The Wallabies are up next. Scotland have won four of their past five against Australia, all under Townsend, and will be expected to make it five from six.

The Wallabies will fancy a crack at them, though. They'll respect Scotland's ability with ball in hand but relish a shot at exposing the weakness in their ranks. You don't need 20-20 vision to spot the frailties in this team. The All Blacks found them with ease in that sobering second-half schooling.

Sports.title: Foggy FA Cup tie: How Altrincham v Notts County was described despite poor visibility
Sports.text:
One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday.

As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two.

"One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience.

"I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the first round and the fog came in.

"Tonight was worse. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing.

"We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging.

"I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can."

National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties.

"The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower.

"It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it.

"Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible."

Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition.

"I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!"

Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window.

"[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower.

"Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Have they changed shape? Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'.

"So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well.

"It was very, very close to getting called off."

Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle.

"It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale.

"You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in."

The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction".

"Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around."

Gaming_Tech.title: Kent M20 crash injures two after more than 30 vehicles collide
Gaming_Tech.text:
More than 30 vehicles were involved in a collision which left two people seriously injured on the M20 in Kent late on Saturday, police say.

Officers were called to the scene at around 18:41 on the London-bound carriageway between junctions eight and nine, near Hollingbourne, Maidstone.

Eleven people were cared for by paramedics and two taken to hospital, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said.

An air ambulance crew, three fire engines and a "technical rescue unit" were sent to the scene, where National Highways said "thick fog" had been confirmed.

The road was shut in both directions early on Sunday and was likely to remain closed "for several hours while recovery and clear up operations continue", the agency said.

Kent Police said one of the two people seriously injured had been taken to a hospital locally, and the other to a London hospital.

"Other drivers have sustained injuries not believed to be serious," it said in a statement.

"Closures are likely to remain overnight while the incident is dealt with."

The force has asked anyone with information about the incident or dashcam footage to come forward.

Gaming_Tech.title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.

But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.

A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.

James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.

"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.

"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.

Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.

The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.

The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.

She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.

Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".

"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

Gaming_Tech.title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.

Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.

It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.

During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.

Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.

"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."

Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.

Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.

In September, GE Aerospace announced, external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.

Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.

Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?

"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.

He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.

But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?

To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".

This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.

Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.

The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.

"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.

Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.

A report in May, external quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.

But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.

China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing, external – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.

Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.

During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane, external, he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.

"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

Gaming_Tech.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
Gaming_Tech.text:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.
