EntertainmentTab.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
EntertainmentTab.text:
Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.

She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

On Thursday, he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Channel 4 Dispatches, Sunday Times and Times programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

Brand is also being investigated over two more rape allegations made by two other women.

Court documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court, held before Brand's criminal trial, suggest one of the women was 16 at the time of the alleged offence and appeared in a Channel 4 documentary. Brand has denied the allegations.

On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.

He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand.

Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry.

Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.

At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."

Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.

After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

EntertainmentTab.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.

He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.

Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.

With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.

He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.

Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.

Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.

The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.

"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."

But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.

"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.

"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."

He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".

The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".

Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".

But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".

In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?

A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."

Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".

"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"

And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".

"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.

At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

We now understand quite how terrible.

EntertainmentTab.title: U2 on Dolly Parton's final duet; and the 'grudge match' behind their new album
EntertainmentTab.text:
U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.

Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).

When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2009 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".

So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.

The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. (Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court.)

U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.

Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.

"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.

"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.

"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.

"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."

For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.

This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever, external since, external.

There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.

Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two, and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.

The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".

There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".

"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.

"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.

"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

During recording sessions last year, Bono told me U2 were chasing "the sound of the future". In a separate interview with Radio 2's Jo Whiley, guitarist The Edge claimed they were working on an album of "sci-fi Irish folk".

The results sure sound like U2, though.

The electronic groove of the opening track, Go (Carnaval de Luz), echoes their experimental 90s phase; while the serrated riffs of Silencio are direct descendants of 2004's Vertigo.

Parton's original lyric was about a woman trying to choose between two men but, with help from Snow Patrol's Jonny McDaid, U2 rewrote the song to address the political divisions tearing families apart.

"Brothers turn to strangers /And sons deny their name / Somebody loses either way And every heart is torn."

Parton recorded her parts in June, less than three months before she died.

"We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal," says Bono.

"That was a real shock. A shock for us because we'd been working with her, but a shock for anyone who loves music.

"I remember I was with [R.E.M. frontman] Michael Stipe in a car when the news came in, and he actually fell down and started sobbing. He just could not believe it.

"Probably the only thing that people can agree on in the entire world right now is Dolly Parton. Whether you're gay or straight or conservative or liberal, she was ready for you to fly at her show."

Another female presence shimmers on the fourth track, The Mirror Maker, which is dedicated to Catalan superstar Rosalía. Written after witnessing her spell-binding Lux tour, Bono describes the "heavens swirling" to reveal "the re-enchantment of the world".

"Normally you have to be dead or in jail for us to write a song about you," he laughs, "but she's a feminine force field. A kind of transcendent, ecstatic musician."

He wrote the song without her knowledge, phoning the singer afterwards to timidly seek her approval.

"It could have been excruciating if she really, really hated it," he grimaces. "I'd have had to pretend it was about Santa Rosalia, a saint who lived in a cave in Italy in the 17th Century."

According to producer Jacknife Lee, The Mirror Maker went through 196 different takes before U2 were happy, suggesting they haven't entirely abandoned their perfectionist streak.

"The early sessions for this album were at times super inspiring, and then really not that good at all," admits The Edge, identifying a stubborn "stick-with-it-ness" that stops them from giving up.

"This band is absolutely relentless," agrees Bono. "It's a grudge match."

"It's the most frustrating thing," Mullen Jr adds. "I'm always reminded of how incapable I am of doing all those things that other people find easy.

"It's always been a challenge for us, and that's what makes those moments when it [works] so special. That's why you keep on chasing it, and why you stay in a band."

There's more to U2's longevity than that, though. Their line-up has remained unchanged since they first formed at Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School 50 years ago. They remain friends first, and superstars second.

When we meet, in a bingo hall that hosted some of U2's formative gigs, there's a familial vibe to the whole operation.

They tease Mullen Jr for turning a hose on fans who climbed the wall of his parents' house in 1976; and chat animatedly about their musical obsessions ("every four-piece wants to be the Beatles," confesses Bono).

Those bonds have kept the band together through commercial and critical ups and downs, not to mention the life-altering injuries that forced Bono to cancel a 2010 US tour, and neck problems that prompted Mullen Jr to skip their 2023-2024 Las Vegas residency.

Doctors advised him to retire, but after a (risky) surgical intervention, he's back behind the kit – developing an entirely new playing style to avoid further damage.

His determination will be put to the test next year, when U2 embark on a massive international stadium tour, including four UK dates at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium next June.

The US leg will see them play some of the same venues as their friend, Ed Sheeran. So what did they make of the controversy over his recent US tour – where some venue owners pressured Sheeran into dropping his support act, Macklemore, for making pro-Palestinian comments?

"We totally support Macklemore's right as an artist to say what he wanted to say," says The Edge.

"I don't think Ed should be vilified. He was in a very difficult situation. But I commend the other young artists who decided to leave [his] tour.

"They were sticking up for an artist's right to free speech, and I think that's the issue above anything else."

He recalls several occasions where U2 themselves made risky political statements on stage.

In 1987, after Arizona's governor banned Martin Luther King Day, Bono faced death threats if he dared to play Pride (In The Name of Love) - which addresses King's assassination - in the state.

He went ahead and did it anyway, closing his eyes in anticipation of a gunshot.

"I looked up at the end of the verse and I clearly wasn't dead," he later told Mojo magazine. 'But not only that... Adam Clayton was standing in front of me."

Similarly, in 1998, the band taunted Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet during a televised concert in Santiago. At the end of the night, they invited the mothers of the victims of Pinochet's 1973 coup d'état on to the stage, who took it in turns to say the names of their children into the microphone.

"It would have been way smarter and better for us to shut up," says the Edge. "But it was artistically necessary, and we just said, 'We can't not do this'."

Reflecting further on the Macklemore controversy, he adds: "We might disagree with some of the members of the pro-Palestine movement, but we absolutely agree with the fundamentals. We absolutely agree that what's going on [in Gaza] is unconscionable and that a child's life is equally valuable, no matter what their background."

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Mullen Jr is equally forthright about the freedom to speak out.

"We, as a band, will fight for the right to speak your mind, as long as it doesn't incite violence," he says.

"Even if we disagree with it or don't like it, nobody - no billionaire, no promoter, no owner - has the right to censor anybody.

"And they will definitely not be censoring us, ever."

Like I said: U2 are at their best when they trust their instincts.

EntertainmentTab.title: Russell Brand: Met Police boss 'wouldn't be surprised' if more allegations made about disgraced star
EntertainmentTab.text:
The head of the Metropolitan Police said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about entertainer and comedian Russell Brand.

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Met Police boss Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

Brand was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday.

Speaking to the BBC, Sir Mark said that he "wouldn't be surprised if more people came forward" about Brand and said there were "two ongoing rape investigations" into him.

Brand has already been interviewed under caution in relation to those allegations.

Sir Mark praised the bravery of the women who came forward to tell their story to the police and during the trial.

"That's a real challenge for anyone having gone through something so ghastly and you have to admire them."

The head of the Met also said that whilst Brand's case "may look different because it's about celebrity, the majority of sex offending is about people abusing power", adding that victims will be believed.

"We will do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful person who is responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life," he said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also spoken about the case, seeking to explain the Labour Party's previous association with Brand, saying "it's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life".

Some within the party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

Now foreign secretary, Miliband has since said he regrets the interview. The BBC has approached Miliband for comment.

In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted in support of Brand on Twitter following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned with.

In his 2014 tweet, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham told the BBC: "His crimes are horrific".

"All I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do."

It was put to Sir Mark during an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's defence barrister "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark said that what he heard reported from the trial was "very close to victim blaming".

Asked whether he would support the Victim's Commissioner's call for a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

He said he would "strongly support" such a decision, adding: "It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case."

Brand was refused bail following his conviction on Thursday and will now spend the weekend in custody before a return to court on Monday for sentencing.

He is expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

Once the trial was over, it was reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Bayles and another member of Brand's staff had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did.

Shortly after, he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager, who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

Bayles said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

Bayles said this was why he decided to stop working with Brand in 2010 and had not had any contact with him since. He added that during his time with Brand, no complaints were made about the entertainer's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

EntertainmentTab.title: Pyre: Indian film on elderly couple's love and loneliness won 18 awards - now it's wowing audiences
EntertainmentTab.text:
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.

The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.

On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.

The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.

Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .

It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.

There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.

"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.

Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".

"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."

Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.

As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.

"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.

With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.

"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.

Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.

Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.

"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."

Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.

"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."

Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.

Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.

Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.

They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.

"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.

But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"

The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".

"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."

Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.

"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

EntertainmentTab.title: Olivia Rodrigo's Christmas song sounds familiar... on purpose
EntertainmentTab.text:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo unwrapped her first-ever Christmas song on Thursday night, alongside a festive music video starring Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon.

The track, called Take Me Home (4 Christmas), finds the pop star asking her boyfriend to "show some serious commitment" by bringing her to his parents' house for the Christmas break.

As soon as it was released, fans noticed similarities to The Waitresses' 1981 festive hit Christmas Wrapping... And it turns out that was by design rather than mistake.

Chris Butler, who wrote The Waitresses' song, posted a message on Facebook, external, saying Rodrigo had contacted him to seek permission for the song; and praising her "phenomenal" writing.

"About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be 'Olivia Rodrigo'," he said. "Said she'd written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it."

Admitting he'd never heard of the pop star before, Butler said he assumed the email was a fake.

But after researching her career, he became a fan - not just of her music, but of the fact she'd hired an all-female band, and negotiated control of her master recordings.

In the end, he decided to reply to her email - and posted the text to his Facebook profile.

"If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering," he said.

"They're really sweet and flattering... even if you AREN'T you.

"If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you, I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them.

He continued: "I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you "got" my songwriting, and that you like our band."

Butler also accepted the invitation to hear Rodrigo's Christmas song, and told his followers: "Her song was/is great.

"It's going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas number one contest they have every year in the UK."

Although the song is indebted to the Waitresses' new wave and post-punk sound, Butler does not receive a writing credit on Take Me Home (4 Christmas) as it neither samples nor interpolates any of his music.

Posting on social media, Rodrigo said it was written last summer with her longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, and Amy Allen, who has previously contributed to songs by Harry Styles, Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McCrae.

Meanwhile, the Christmas jumper-tastic video, external follows the single's storyline, with SNL star Ben Marshall playing her feckless boyfriend, and Nixon starring as her prospective mother-in-law.

EntertainmentTab.title: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'
EntertainmentTab.text:
British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.

DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally".

"If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.

Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023, "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.

Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK.

It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.

Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped.

"I want to find solutions," he says.

"Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."

Allstar has long been a champion of UK rap and currently presents the Rap Show on BBC Radio 1, which he describes as "the show I always wanted as a kid".

This new role is "a pinch me moment," he says.

The Official Charts Company previously listed the 40 top selling R&B and hip hop tracks on its website, but there had been nowhere for fans to listen to the chart.

"It was literally just a bunch of numbers and text, so it kind of existed but not in this capacity," Allstar says.

GeneralTab.text:

GeneralTab.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
GeneralTab.text:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.

Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.

Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.

In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.

Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.

"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.

That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler committed suicide: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."

The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.

But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.

Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.

"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.

Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.

"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.

Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".

Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.

Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".

"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.

Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.

With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.

A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.

In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.

The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.

But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.

As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

GeneralTab.title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
GeneralTab.text:
No one who served in the UK armed forces should have to sleep on the streets this Christmas, Andy Burnham has said.

Downing Street said the PM would personally write to councils across England on Armistice Day (11 November) to urge them to draw up plans to offer accommodation for veterans sleeping rough ahead of the festive period.

He will say that national and local government should work under the "simple principle" that "no one who has served our country should ever be left to sleep rough on our streets".

The Conservatives have meanwhile criticised Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy for seeming to link participation in an EU scheme for young people with the armed forces' sacrifices on Remembrance Sunday.

Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional £874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans.

"People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday.

"When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."

The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.

Downing Street said an additional £8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.

Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.

The pledge, announced ahead of Remembrance Sunday, is part of Burnham's wider plan to offer everyone currently sleeping rough a bed this winter.

The most recent official figures estimated that there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England - a record high. The number of people recorded as sleeping rough has been on the rise since 2021.

The government has committed £4.4bn in total to end rough sleeping.

Burnham previously faced criticism from the Conservatives for failing to end rough sleeping while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester.

He argued that Manchester's scheme attracted rough sleepers from the surrounding regions, adding that "it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping".

Liberal Democrats defence spokesman James MacCleary MP said the funding was an "important first step" but that "a one-off cash injection won't fix a crisis years in the making".

He urged Burnham to guarantee long-term funding for councils to tackle homelessness "for good" and to put in place measures to prevent veterans "falling through the cracks in the first place".

The prime minister is urging any veterans who are sleeping rough, or those supporting them, to call a UK-wide helpline on 0800 9520774 to be connected directly to housing and other specialist support.

Separately on Sunday, the culture secretary set out the UK's renewed participation in the EU's Erasmus programme of educational and cultural exchanges for young people after six years.

The UK will rejoin the programme in January, enabling students and other young people to study, train or get work experience in the EU.

In the announcement, Nandy added: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake responded by saying veterans had not fought for a "student exchange scheme".

He argued that it was "tone deaf and frankly shameful" to announce this on Remembrance Sunday.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," the Tory chairman added.

GeneralTab.title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
GeneralTab.text:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.

Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.

"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.

"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

GeneralTab.title: Why should I care if share prices fall?
GeneralTab.text:
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.

The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.

As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.

Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.

Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.

Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.

Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.

Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.

Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.

Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.

So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.

Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.

Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.

Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.

In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.

Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.

As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.

Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.

That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.

However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.

If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.

That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.

When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.

There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.

In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).

However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.

Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.

Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.

So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.

When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.

As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.

Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

The most recent official figures estimated that there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England - a record high. The number of people recorded as sleeping rough has been on the rise since 2021.

The government has committed £4.4bn in total to end rough sleeping.

Burnham previously faced criticism from the Conservatives for failing to end rough sleeping while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester.

He argued that Manchester's scheme attracted rough sleepers from the surrounding regions, adding that "it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping".

Liberal Democrats defence spokesman James MacCleary MP said the funding was an "important first step" but that "a one-off cash injection won't fix a crisis years in the making".

He urged Burnham to guarantee long-term funding for councils to tackle homelessness "for good" and to put in place measures to prevent veterans "falling through the cracks in the first place".

The prime minister is urging any veterans who are sleeping rough, or those supporting them, to call a UK-wide helpline on 0800 9520774 to be connected directly to housing and other specialist support.

Separately on Sunday, the culture secretary set out the UK's renewed participation in the EU's Erasmus programme of educational and cultural exchanges for young people after six years.

The UK will rejoin the programme in January, enabling students and other young people to study, train or get work experience in the EU.

In the announcement, Nandy added: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake responded by saying veterans had not fought for a "student exchange scheme".

He argued that it was "tone deaf and frankly shameful" to announce this on Remembrance Sunday.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," the Tory chairman added.

articles.title: Royal Family join veterans and families at Festival of Remembrance
articles.text:
King Charles III led senior members of the Royal Family as they paid tribute to British service personnel at this year's Festival of Remembrance.

The Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales, joined the King and Queen Camilla at London's Royal Albert Hall to commemorate those who lost their lives in service, on the eve of Remembrance Sunday.

The audience stood and a fanfare played as the royals entered the concert hall for the annual event, which was also attended by bereaved families and serving personnel.

The King will lead the nation in two minutes of silence on Sunday to remember those who died serving in the two world wars and other conflicts.

He will be joined by other senior royals and political leaders at the annual National Service of Remembrance ceremony at the Cenotaph in central London, where they will lay wreaths.

Some 10,000 veterans will take part in the Royal British Legion's march-past, representing more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations.

The Royal British Legion's festival, which was broadcast on BBC One at 21:00, was hosted by Clive Myrie and included performances by musicians such as Alfie Boe and Mica Paris.

The Chelsea Pensioners - retired British Army veterans - were also among those in attendance, while several armed forces bands took to the stage to perform, including the Band of Royal Air Force Regiment.

This year's festival marks the 35th anniversary of the end of the First Gulf War and 15 years since the conclusion of British military operations in Iraq under Operation Telic, with veterans sharing their personal stories and experiences of the conflicts.

Last year, Prince George joined the King, Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales at the concert for what was thought to be the first time.

articles.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn’t expect a smooth ride
articles.text:
Déjà vu? The Eurostar has been booked. Strategic leaks of draft agreements have started.

The EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier is warning the UK it can't have it all and it will not be able to rejoin its single market "à la carte".

Naturally, there is even a row about smoky bacon crisps – an argument between the UK and EU about food labelling has become a classic of the genre. Remember the bendy banana? Or the so-called sausage war between Boris Johnson and Emmanuel Macron?

It's a clash between those arguing it's worth swallowing some new rules to ease trade with the continent, or those whose message to Brussels is, "hands off our snacks" - even though we are not actually in the EU anymore.

Andy Burnham's big moment with the bloc top brass is fast approaching - the second annual EU-UK Summit since the UK's withdrawal from the EU takes place in Brussels on 20 November.

That meeting is not supposed to be about whether the UK might one day go back in. The prime minister has suggested that is his long-term ambition - but is he really ready for what is to come?

First, Burnham inherited the broad deal that's likely to be signed. The UK and EU were originally meant to mint a new and, they hope, improved agreement back in May, then in July, and well, political upheavals mean one thing for getting things done – delay.

But that means the outlines of a new agreement have been clear for many months, an approach based on "closer alignment" as Sir Keir Starmer proclaimed to us at the start of the year.

So if the prime minister hails agreement, spare a thought for those who started the work to get it this far many months ago.

One source familiar with the negotiations told me, "They are 90% there", with agreements designed to make life easier for food producers, a deal on emissions trading which could help manufacturers, and new arrangements for youth visas (although it's understood there is still haggling over putting a cap on the numbers).

An EU source close to the process said: "The bone of contention is a cap – we proposed 150,000, the UK proposed 50,000 – but we would expect to reach a compromise", even though it has been "very tense" on both sides.

A last-minute call from the EU to cut tuition fees for its students is expected to be parked for now with more months of discussion to come. Another fine tradition - agree what you can, but file some tough stuff away for future chat.

There are dilemmas too on the EU's so-called "Made in Europe" plans – draft laws to protect its industries from being hammered by Chinese competition. The purpose is clear – to help the economy grow, with the prime minister quoting figures that suggest closer ties to the EU without going back in could add 0.4 percent to GDP.

But as the tabloid-friendly row over salty snacks illustrates, making it easier to do business with the bloc doesn't come without a cost, and a political awkwardness.

Talking to my colleague, the BBC's Business editor Simon Jack this week, the prime minister admitted the UK would have to follow more EU rules. "That's where we've ended up," Burnham acknowledged.

And whatever your feelings on the matter, that lands us slap-bang back in the middle of the eternal dilemma of the relationship between the UK and the European Union.

How much control is the UK willing to lose in the hope of bigger wins? Even when it comes to a relatively limited number of important issues that are on the table in the current discussions?

The prime minister has scrapped the limits of this troubled conversation, not just suggesting a closer relationship with the relatively dry and technical changes being discussed right now, but dangling the possibility of going back into the bloc one day.

Suggesting freedom of movement again, unlimited immigration for Brits who want to live or work on the continent and vice versa. That's after repeated promises, including from him, that that sometimes toxic debate would not be reopened.

What is he up to? It seems the prime minister's main line of thinking is that with problems like long passport queues and red tape for business it is right and proper to try to sort them out.

That is after all, what Rishi Sunak and then Sir Keir Starmer tried to do.

But his willingness to contemplate going a lot further is based on a belief that the public's attitude has shifted – if you look at polling it does suggest that a majority of voters support going back into the EU, external.

It just so happens his own long-time conviction is to go back into the bloc one day. And that idea chimes not just with many Labour activists and members, but also with the Lib Dems, Greens and SNP – whose voters he'd be only too happy to peel off.

But hang on, don't let Burnham's easy-breezy style mask that just casually mentioning he is open to us going back into the EU in the run up to this summit is a huge and difficult thing. Whatever relationship he truly wants to seek, and even those involved in the conversations aren't quite sure he is even sure, don't expect a smooth ride from the EU.

In an interview you can see tomorrow, the EU's chief negotiator last time, Michel Barnier, told me the UK cannot pick and choose the relationship "à la carte".

If we wanted to go back in, he told me, the UK could forget the famous rebate, and there is no way to be in the huge trading bloc, the single market, without accepting freedom of movement.

One government figure told me, even now dealing with the EU there are "lots of very warm words, but quite a lot of arms folded".

An EU insider told me the mood has certainly changed. "There is big scope getting closer to the EU, but nobody wants it to be toxic… we wonder, does he know what he is doing?"

Last time round, the majority of businesses, with some notable noisy outliers, were keen to stay in the EU. But after several years having to make the relationship work, and spend money on rearranging how they do business, that might not translate into such solid support if the prime minister does choose to pursue a return to the EU.

One prominent business figure explains: "You're a langoustine exporter from Ullapool? Yes, please. You are manufacturing and making that car? Yes, get me back in. You're a drugs manufacturer? Well, sort of, yes and no. You're in financial services? We've spent the money. Do we want to unpick this?"

There are prominent backers of the idea of a return to the EU, if Burnham himself decides to make that case. The former Chancellor Rachel Reeves and the London Mayor Sadiq Khan make the case as well.

We've already talked about the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP, and Plaid Cymru being up for it, as are many Labour MPs and ministers.

But the political risks of arguing for a return to the union are, frankly, enormous. Labour is divided, just as the country could be, whatever the current polls suggest.

One former Labour minister told me, "the prime minister wants us to go back in, but it is a very hazardous route", saying of the party's broadly pro-European rank and file: "Nobody wants to criticise Andy, but if it blows open they won't all be in the same place".

One cabinet minister's eyes rolled so violently when I asked if they fancied another referendum they nearly went into the back of their head. And it is a safe bet that if the prime minister really decides to pursue a return that there'd be a ferocious pushback from the other side.

The Conservatives and Reform are already howling with protest about the deal expected to be signed this month.

Kemi Badenoch criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum" adding, "he is not going to get a better deal… it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand."

Meanwhile Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door", and said Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".

And you can expect similar financial arguments to be made as last time round. Vote Leave was always only too happy to have noisy clashes over the cash the UK paid to be part of the EU – that £350m – the gross contribution, not the net.

But every argument about the amount reminded the public that the UK did spend millions, even if the figure was officially judged as misleading.

While EU leaders might want to be helpful to Burnham, the Czech prime minister's comments on the issue were rather unhelpful. Asked recently if he'd like to see the UK go back his answer was, "Yes, of course – we need more money".

There could be enormous opportunity for the economy, important support for the UK's security, and a boost for the prime minister's backing among some voters if he does indeed end up deciding he will make the case for the UK to rejoin the European Union.

But it would be a heck of a gamble. A decade ago, a relatively popular prime minister named David Cameron with expert communication skills wanted to reset the UK's relationship with the EU. That blew up his leadership, unleashing a series of political disasters that saw him off, and dogged his party for years.

Andy Burnham is a relatively popular prime minister too, also confident in his ability to communicate with you, and serious about improving our ties with the EU. But in his party, there are those preaching caution about opening this conversation.

The successes or failures of the impending summit will give him, and the rest of us, a taste of what might lie ahead.

articles.title: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary
articles.text:
US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post.

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"

It was unclear whether the president's public job offer was genuine, although White said later on Saturday: "I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday".

The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days into the job.

Trump's post on Saturday afternoon comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.

The president called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country".

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters.

Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room.

"On to the next chapter," White wrote, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek.

"Hell yeah! Do it, @DanaWhite!" White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X, as he shared the president's message.

White was ringside for a fight in London on Saturday night between British former world champion Chris Billam-Smith and Jamaican-born Briton Cheavon Clarke at the Copper Box Arena.

Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference afterwards, the UFC chief executive said he was flying to Washington for a meeting with Trump on Monday.

"I got a lot of jobs already," he told reporters.

"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he added, without being drawn on whether he was interested in taking on one of the most gruelling jobs in the political arena.

CNN cited a source familiar as saying that White had declined the idea.

As he noted in the news conference, he already has a number of time-consuming commitments.

As well as leading UFC and Power Slap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, he has just launched Zuffa Boxing, a professional promotion company.

And last year he was unveiled as one of three new board members of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.

He released a clip in 2020 lambasting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights during the pandemic.

In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to credential rules backstage at UFC events.

White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.

When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport's future seemed uncertain.

Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states.

"None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White said in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."

With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.

White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.

This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.
